title: The Cosmic Jewels of Sextans A
caption: The dwarf galaxy Sextans A, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Data obtained and processed by: P. Massey (Lowell Obs.), G. Jacoby, K. Olsen, & C. Smith (AURA/NSF). Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Bright young stars glitter across Sextans A, an irregular dwarf galaxy whose roughly square outline stands out in this image from Kitt Peak National Observatory's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope. It lies around 4.4 million light-years from Earth.
That odd outline has been twisted into shape by successive waves of supernova explosions. Sextans A is only a fraction of the Milky Way's size, measuring just about 5000 light-years across.

Irregular galaxies lack the orderly look of spirals or ellipticals and come in all sorts of strange shapes. They are relatively small, and they are often vulnerable to being pulled out of shape by close encounters or collisions with larger galaxies, which can sometimes explain their irregular forms. For Sextans A, the shaping is attributed to its own exploding stars. Bright young stars, like the ones sparkling here, are a sign that the galaxy is still forming new generations.
scale: Sextans A lies around 4.4 million light-years from Earth and measures about 5000 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
